topic: 12 Multi-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: What en route performance requirement applies to a multi-engine Class B aeroplane?

options.text: After one engine fails, it can reach a safe forced landing site
It can climb at 300 ft/min after an engine failure
It can hold its cruise level after an engine failure
After one engine fails, it can reach 1 000 ft above a suitable aerodrome

explanation: With one engine failed and the others within maximum continuous power, it must be able to continue at or above the minimum safe altitudes to a point 1 000 ft above an aerodrome where it can land.

topic: 12 Multi-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: How does the multi-engine Class B en route rule differ from the single-engine rule?

options.text: It requires a higher cruising level
It needs an aerodrome, not a field
It requires two alternate aerodromes on every route
There is no difference

explanation: A single must reach a place for a safe forced landing; a twin, with one engine still working, must be able to continue to an aerodrome and land.

topic: 12 Multi-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: Which two distances must be known to plan compliance with the multi-engine Class B en route rule?

options.text: The all-engines cruise range and the glide range
The take-off distance and the landing distance
The one-engine descent range and the one-engine cruise range
The distance to the alternate and the reserve fuel distance remaining

explanation: The one-engine-inoperative descent (drift down) range plus the one-engine cruise range give the total range after an engine failure.

topic: 12 Multi-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: What is the highest altitude that may be assumed for the en route rule?

options.text: Where all-engines MCP climb is 300 ft/min
The absolute ceiling with one engine inoperative
Where the one-engine-inoperative rate of climb falls to 300 ft/min

explanation: The aeroplane may not be assumed to be above the altitude where the all-engines rate of climb at maximum continuous power equals 300 ft/min.

topic: 12 Multi-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: For the en route rule, how is a one-engine-inoperative gross descent gradient adjusted?

options.text: Multiplied by 0.77
Reduced by 0.5%
Increased by 0.5%
Increased by 1.1%

explanation: The net descent gradient is the gross descent gradient increased by 0.5%; a net climb gradient is the gross climb gradient reduced by 0.5%.

topic: 12 Multi-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: The one-engine-inoperative gross climb gradient is 1.2%. What net gradient is used?

topic: 12 Multi-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: The one-engine-inoperative gross descent gradient is 2%. What net gradient is used?
explanation: Net descent gradient = gross + 0.5% = 2.5%. The steeper assumed descent gives a shorter, safer range.

topic: 12 Multi-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: After an engine failure in the cruise, why must a twin descend?

options.text: The aeroplane becomes heavier
Thrust can no longer balance drag
The pressurisation fails
The remaining engine overheats at high altitude in the cruise

explanation: With one engine failed, drag exceeds thrust, so to hold speed (ideally VMD) the nose must be lowered, using a component of weight to balance the excess drag.

topic: 12 Multi-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: At which speed is the drift down normally flown?

options.text: VMP
VMO
VY
VMD

explanation: Flying at VMD keeps the excess drag, and so the descent angle, as small as possible.

topic: 12 Multi-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: During the drift down, why does the descent angle become shallower?

options.text: The pilot reduces the speed below VMD
The aeroplane gets heavier as it descends into denser air
Denser air at lower levels gives more thrust from the live engine
Drag rises as the aeroplane descends

explanation: As the aeroplane descends into denser air the remaining engine produces more thrust, so less weight component is needed and the nose can be raised gradually.

topic: 12 Multi-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: When does the drift down end?

options.text: After a fixed 10 minutes
When thrust balances drag again
When the aeroplane reaches 1 500 ft above the ground below
When the speed falls to VMP

explanation: The aeroplane descends until the remaining engine produces enough thrust to balance drag without help from the weight component, then levels off.

topic: 12 Multi-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: Without a drift down graph, how is the drift down range calculated?

options.text: By splitting the profile into segments and adding their distances
By using the single-engine glide formula
By dividing the total height by the gross gradient just once
By multiplying the cruise range by 0.77

explanation: Because the gradient keeps changing, the profile is split into segments, each with its own net gradient and height; their distances are added.

topic: 12 Multi-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: A drift down is split into two segments: 9 000 to 7 000 ft at a net gradient of 3%, and 7 000 to 5 000 ft at 2%. What is the total distance?

options.text: About 33.0 NM
About 2.7 NM
About 22.0 NM
About 27.4 NM

topic: 12 Multi-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: How is the total one-engine-inoperative range found for route planning?

options.text: Drift down plus OEI cruise range
Drift down range only
Glide range with both engines failed and propellers feathered
All-engines range minus 50%

explanation: After the drift down the aeroplane can cruise level on one engine, so the cruise range is added to the descent range.

topic: 12 Multi-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: How is the en route rule shown on a route chart?

options.text: The track avoids all terrain above 5 000 ft
The track stays within 60 minutes of any aerodrome
The track stays within circles of total one-engine range around aerodromes
The track stays within glide range of open fields along the route

explanation: Circles with the total one-engine range as radius are drawn around each usable aerodrome; the track must stay inside them so a landing is always reachable.

topic: 12 Multi-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: Why must the net descent range, not the gross range, be used when planning?

options.text: It is always longer than the gross range
It contains a safety margin
It is the only range figure published in the flight manual
It includes the wind

explanation: The extra 0.5% gradient makes the planned range shorter than the expected gross range, giving a margin.

topic: 12 Multi-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: Above the 300 ft/min altitude, how is the extra height used in the en route calculation?

options.text: It may be used if the weather is VMC
It is converted at 0.77 of its value
It may be used in full
It may not be used to extend the planned range

explanation: The aeroplane may fly higher, but the planning may not take credit for height above the 300 ft/min altitude.
